prompt: I am trying to sanity check MinIO’s policy enforcement from a security perspective, and I have a nagging worry that a principal who should be read only might still be able to mutate data through some less obvious S3 surface area when the system is under stress. Could you set up a minimal reproduction where one identity is supposed to have read only access to a bucket and prefix, while other clients are hammering the same bucket with normal writes and metadata traffic, and then show what actually happens when the read only identity tries things that feel adjacent to writes like multipart operations, copy style writes, metadata changes, or deletes, plus what metadata can be learned from listing and HEAD behavior without full reads? I am looking for concrete runtime evidence in the form of request and response traces and observed storage side effects that demonstrates whether the boundary really holds or whether there is a bypass hiding in the corners. Temporary scripts may be used for observation, but the repository itself should remain unchanged and anything temporary should be cleaned up afterward.
